job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Tara Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher at the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a room in a three-person flat in Manchester, and my days are weirdly organised because I love a spreadsheet. I track every application in one: company, date, stage, who I spoke to. I finished an information systems degree in June with a pass. My final project was a stock-and-orders tool for a local bakery, which the owner, Mrs Okeke, still uses on Tuesdays. I apply, I practise interview questions with my flatmate Priya, and I do a few hours of shifts at the bakery on Saturdays.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy most about building something like that bakery tool?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the first in my family to do a degree. My dad drives a bus and my mum cleans offices, so they're proud but don't know how any of it works. They've topped up my rent a few times and told me not to rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's about what I figured. People get excited about each new tool and then it becomes another thing in the toolbar. I'd laugh with Priya and say my spreadsheet outlives the hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my job search is the same slog but nothing is racing me. I've no internship, and a pass, so I'm in the pile. There are plenty of jobs in Manchester though, and my parents and my savings give me time. The thing that bugs me is paying rent on a room when I thought I'd be earning by now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going: eight applications a week, a follow-up email to each, and one local meetup a month. I'd ask Mrs Okeke to write a short reference and to let me list the bakery tool as a real client project. I'd use an AI model now and then to tidy my cover letter, and check every line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not dramatic, just that low hum of everyone else being further along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said everyone else is further along. Who do you compare yourself to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Marcus, who started at a bank in September. And the group chat from my course, where people post their start dates. I know I shouldn't look at my course group chat, but I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changed after you asked Mrs Okeke for a reference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She cried a bit, which was awkward, and then wrote two paragraphs I could actually use. It made me see a real customer is worth more than a lecturer's line. I'd forgotten it counted.

say: I'd tell Priya my **spreadsheet** will outlive the hype.
I'd say the new tools become another button in the toolbar.
think: The job search is the same **slog**, with no internship and a pass.
Rent on a room while I still earn nothing is what **bugs** me.
do: Send **eight applications a week**, each with a follow-up email.
Ask Mrs Okeke for a **reference** and list the bakery tool as a real client project.
feel: **Uneasy**, a low hum of everyone else being further along.
S0.quote: I know I shouldn't look at my course group chat, but I do.
fieldNote: Compares herself with **course mates** and a cousin, which feeds her unease.
The **bakery** customer is her best reference and she nearly forgot it.
Uses AI lightly and **checks** every line.

steps.text: Send eight applications a week and email a follow-up to each
Use an AI model to tidy cover letters, then check every line

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's the realistic picture. Writing, checking, booking and planning are most of what an information systems graduate does on day one. I'd tell my course friends to get ready for a world where the juniors are fewer and each does more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think it's aimed at people like me. The junior analyst role, where you take notes, build a report, tidy a dataset, is what the software does best. A firm that used to hire six of us might hire two and keep one extra senior to supervise the tool. I'm a pass with no internship, so I'm not top of anyone's pile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for jobs where the human part matters: client support, implementation, onboarding. That's where I can sit with Mrs Okeke types and sort out the mess. I'd do a short course in a business tool, like a CRM or a process-mapping certificate, and tell interviewers I can teach people to use the software. I'd also take a fixed-term contract rather than wait for a permanent role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not yet scared, but I've got that feeling you get before an exam you can't fully prepare for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather be the person who teaches people the software. Why that role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because tools don't sit with a customer who's cross at a screen. I've done it with Mrs Okeke when her orders went missing. It's a skill I didn't know I had until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your family fit into this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum would say get a council job, because it's secure. Dad would say try the buses, which is a joke. They don't get that a gap year is not an option now. I'd tell them it's a different market, not a failure.

say: I'd tell my course friends the juniors will be **fewer**, each doing more.
I'd say the realistic picture is writing, checking and planning going first.
think: The **junior analyst** role is what the software does best.
A firm that hired six might hire **two**, and I'm not top of anyone's pile.
do: Apply for **client support and onboarding** roles where the human part matters.
Take a **fixed-term contract** and a short CRM certificate rather than wait.
feel: **Anxious**, like before an exam I can't fully prepare for.
S1.quote: Tools don't sit with a customer who's cross at a screen. I've done it with Mrs Okeke when her orders went missing.
fieldNote: She sees her **bakery** experience as proof of a people skill.
Steady adopter: moves toward **human-facing** roles before the tools force it.
Family advice comes from **security** thinking that no longer fits.

steps.text: Apply for client support, implementation and onboarding roles
Complete a CRM or process-mapping certificate in three months
Keep doing paid Saturday shifts and tool fixes for the bakery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is mad and no one is ready. Two years is nothing. I'd tell my parents it's not like previous technology waves, and I'd probably say it badly because I'd be panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it might be the end of the road I planned. Entry-level information jobs are mostly thinking work, so they'd be the first to go. Robots for hands-on stuff come about 2031, so my dad's bus and my mum's cleaning would last longer than my own career. That sounds ridiculous but it's what I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get any work that pays rent within weeks, including bakery shifts full time. I'd talk to my parents about moving back home to save the rent, though I'd hate it. I'd put what I have in a savings account and cut anything extra. I'd also look at the rail depot and the council, since those hire people even in slow patches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel like the one thing I worked for has been moved out of reach just as I reached for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your parents' jobs would last longer than your career. How would you feel saying that to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Weird and guilty. Dad's been proud I'm in a 'clean' job. I'd say it quietly while we do the dishes, and he'd probably tell me to stop being daft, then lie awake like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the first thing you'd cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Takeaway on Fridays, then the gym, then the group trips with Priya. I'd keep my phone and my train pass. It's depressing how fast I can list them.

say: I'd say **two years** is nothing and tell my parents this wave is different.
I'd probably say it badly because I'd be panicking.
think: Entry-level information jobs are **thinking work**, so they go first.
My parents' jobs on the **bus and cleaning** might outlast my career.
do: Take **any work** that pays rent within weeks, including full-time bakery shifts.
Look at the **council and rail depot**, and consider moving back home to save.
feel: **Alarmed**: the thing I worked for moved out of reach.
S2.quote: My dad's bus and my mum's cleaning would last longer than my own career. That sounds ridiculous but it's what I think.
fieldNote: Reverses the **ladder** she was sold: manual work outlasts her clean job.
Reaches for **security** (council, rail) despite earlier rejection of it.
Guilt toward her **parents** drives much of the alarm.

steps.text: Take full-time bakery shifts while I look for steadier work
Move back to my parents' home to save rent
Cut takeaways, the gym and the Friday group trips
Put my savings into a plain account and leave them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real chance, but only if people plan. I'd say firms and governments should publish what jobs they think will change, like a weather report. I'd say this at my flat dinners and online for the three people who care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel better. In five years I could be a person with three years' experience, someone who has done real jobs and has stories. Robots for hands-on stuff come about 2034, so I'd say the ground work is safer longer than my sort of desk work. It's still a scary clock, but it's a clock I can plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any decent first job inside six months and ask for every project that touches customers. I'd start a part-time diploma in project management, since people are needed to run things. I'd save 250 a month and put half of it into a basic index fund, and keep the rest in cash. I'd learn the AI tools properly, not just for letters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but organised. I'd put it in a spreadsheet, honestly, with dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put the clock in a spreadsheet. What would be in it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Columns for savings, skills, contacts, and a column called 'what if I'm wrong'. Every month I'd fill it in. A spreadsheet stops the worry swirling around in my head and turns it into something I can look at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the 'what if I'm wrong' column like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's where I write what I'd do if my job vanished in year three instead of year five. Last time I did that, the answer was bakery, council, or move home. Not great, but it's a plan.

say: I'd say firms and governments should publish a **jobs weather report**.
I'd say five years is a real chance, but only with a plan.
think: I could have **three years' experience** by 2031 and stories to tell.
Ground work stays safer than desk work until about **2034**.
do: Take a decent **first job** in six months and ask for customer-facing projects.
Start a part-time **project management diploma** and save 250 a month.
feel: **Uneasy but organised**, with the worry put into a spreadsheet.
S3.quote: A spreadsheet stops the worry swirling around in my head and turns it into something I can look at.
fieldNote: Turns worry into a **spreadsheet**, true to her habits.
Plans for being **wrong**, which fits a steady adopter.
Mixes **cash and index funds**, cautious but not frozen.

steps.text: Take any decent first job within six months
Start a part-time project management diploma
Save 250 a month, half in cash and half in an index fund
Keep a monthly savings and skills spreadsheet with a back-up plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's take AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to get a real career going, so I'd tell friends to relax a bit and still keep learning. I'd say jobs will change but we've got room to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I could work, move up, maybe move cities, and have a bit saved. By 2036 I'd be 33 and have changed jobs once or twice. Even if AGI arrives, I'd have experience and a few contacts. Robots for hands-on work would only come by 2039, so most of my working life so far would still be intact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start at a firm that does something real, like logistics or health, and learn how a business runs. I'd study part-time, maybe a degree top-up in data or in management. I'd save, and I'd help my parents by paying off their small loan. I'd also learn the AI tools on the job, step by step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. I'd have the usual money worries, rent and the future, but not the 'everything is ending' one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd pay off your parents' loan. How did that come up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They took one for my laptop and my course books, about 3,000. They never mention it, but I see the statement on the table sometimes. Clearing my parents' loan for my laptop and course books would feel like a proper graduation to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could spoil this calm picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A recession in year three. The ten years doesn't protect you from an ordinary bad year. I'd want a few months of savings and a skill that's useful in a downturn.

say: I'd tell friends to **relax a bit** and keep learning.
I'd say jobs will change but we have room to move.
think: Even if AGI arrives, I'd have **experience** and contacts by 2036.
Robots for hands-on work only arrive by **2039**.
do: Start at a firm doing something **real**, like logistics or health.
**Pay off** my parents' 3,000 loan and study part-time in data or management.
feel: **Fairly calm**, with ordinary rent and future worries only.
S4.quote: Clearing my parents' loan for my laptop and course books would feel like a proper graduation to me.
fieldNote: Her **family** debt is a small but vivid goal.
Worries about an ordinary **recession** more than AGI in this picture.
Wants a skill that holds in a **downturn**.

steps.text: Start at a logistics or health firm and learn how it runs
Study a part-time data or management top-up
Pay off my parents' 3,000 loan and keep three months saved

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because my sort of job is thinking work and it would go first. What would help is a guaranteed place on a paid training scheme and a clear promise from the government on what happens to people between jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say people think graduates are spoiled. A lot of us are first-generation, we're anxious and we're doing everything right. Please don't call that entitled.

headlineQuote: A lot of us are first-generation, we're anxious and we're doing everything right. Please don't call that entitled.
portrait: Tara is **23**, an information systems graduate with a pass, renting a room in Manchester and tracking every application in a spreadsheet.
She is **first in her family** to graduate; her parents, a bus driver and a cleaner, give small top-ups.
She is a steady adopter who uses AI **now and then** and prefers human-facing roles where software needs a person.
Her mood runs from uneasy to **alarmed** in the 2028 picture, because her kind of desk work is what goes first.
She copes by **planning**: spreadsheets, back-up plans, and a part-time diploma.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture worries her most because her kind of thinking work would go first.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed place on a **paid training scheme** and a clear promise about what happens between jobs.
